summary.text: Take \(n=33085221781504=2^{14}\cdot4409\cdot458009\), where \(4409\) and \(458009\) are prime; multiplicativity and prime-power divisor-sum formulas give \(\sum_{d\mid n}d=66183576284700\) and \(\sum_{d\mid n}\sigma_1(d)=132367152569399\). Hence \(a(n)=2(66183576284700)-132367152569399=1\), although \(n\ne1,12\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
\sigma(r)=\sum_{e\mid r}e
\]
denote the sum of the positive divisors of \(r\). The deficiency used in the definition of A296075 is
\[
\delta(r)=2r-\sigma(r),
\]
so the sequence is
\[
a(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}\delta(d)
     =\sum_{d\mid n}\bigl(2d-\sigma(d)\bigr).
\]
We will exhibit a positive integer other than \(1\) and \(12\) for which this sum is \(1\).

Take
\[
N=33085221781504=2^{14}\cdot 4409\cdot 458009.
\]
Indeed, \(2^{14}=16384\), \(4409\cdot458009=2019361681\), and their product is \(33085221781504\).

We first record that the two odd factors are prime. This can, for example, be proved by the following short sequence of Lucas order computations. We include the details so that the use of the prime-factor divisor formulas below is justified.

We use this elementary criterion: suppose \(m>1\), the complete prime factorization of \(m-1\) is known, and an integer \(g\) satisfies
\[
g^{m-1}\equiv1\pmod m,
\]
whereas
\[
g^{(m-1)/q}\not\equiv1\pmod m
\]
for every prime \(q\mid m-1\). Then \(m\) is prime. To see this, the first congruence implies that \(g\) is a unit modulo \(m\). Its multiplicative order divides \(m-1\). If that order were a proper divisor of \(m-1\), then for some prime \(q\mid m-1\) it would divide \((m-1)/q\), contrary to the second set of congruences. Thus the order is exactly \(m-1\). The group of units modulo \(m\) consequently has at least \(m-1\) elements. Since there are only \(m-1\) nonzero residue classes, every nonzero residue class is a unit. This is possible only when \(m\) is prime.

The needed factorizations of \(m-1\) and modular powers are as follows. All the displayed modular powers are obtained by ordinary repeated squaring. In each row, the first residue says \(g^{m-1}\equiv1\pmod m\); after it, for every distinct prime factor \(q\) of \(m-1\), the residue of \(g^{(m-1)/q}\) is displayed.

\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c}
m&m-1&g&g^{m-1}\bmod m&q:\ g^{(m-1)/q}\bmod m\\ \hline
19&2\cdot3^2&2&1&2:18,\quad3:7\\
29&2^2\cdot7&2&1&2:28,\quad7:16\\
229&2^2\cdot3\cdot19&6&1&2:228,\quad3:134,\quad19:165\\
57251&2\cdot5^3\cdot229&2&1&2:57250,\quad5:55371,\quad229:48088\\
4409&2^3\cdot19\cdot29&3&1&2:4408,\quad19:209,\quad29:3965\\
458009&2^3\cdot57251&3&1&2:458008,\quad57251:6561
\end{array}
\]

None of the residues in the last column is \(1\). Starting with the evident primes \(2,3,5,7\), the criterion therefore proves successively that \(19\) and \(29\) are prime, then that \(229\) is prime, then that \(57251\) is prime, and finally that both \(4409\) and \(458009\) are prime. They are distinct odd primes, so \(2^{14}\), \(4409\), and \(458009\) are pairwise coprime.

We now evaluate the two divisor sums that occur in \(a(N)\). First,
\[
a(N)=2\sum_{d\mid N}d-\sum_{d\mid N}\sigma(d).
\]
This follows simply by distributing the sum in the definition of \(a(N)\).

For pairwise coprime positive integers, every divisor of their product is uniquely a product of one divisor of each factor. Hence the sum-of-divisors function is multiplicative on coprime factors. Since the prime-power factorization of \(N\) is
\[
N=2^{14}\cdot4409\cdot458009,
\]
we get
\[
\sum_{d\mid N}d
 =\left(\sum_{i=0}^{14}2^i\right)(1+4409)(1+458009).
\]
The geometric sum is
\[
\sum_{i=0}^{14}2^i=2^{15}-1=32767.
\]
Thus
\[
\sum_{d\mid N}d=32767\cdot4410\cdot458010.
\]
The first two factors multiply to
\[
32767\cdot4410=144502470,
\]
and therefore
\[
\sum_{d\mid N}d
 =144502470\cdot458010
 =66183576284700.
\]

It remains to evaluate \(\sum_{d\mid N}\sigma(d)\). Recall that \(\sigma\) itself is multiplicative on coprime arguments: if \(x\) and \(y\) are coprime, every divisor of \(xy\) is uniquely \(uv\) with \(u\mid x\), \(v\mid y\), and therefore
\[
\sigma(xy)=\sum_{u\mid x}\sum_{v\mid y}uv
          =\sigma(x)\sigma(y).
\]
Every divisor of \(N\) has a unique form
\[
d=2^i4409^j458009^k,
\qquad 0\le i\le14,\quad j,k\in\{0,1\}.
\]
By multiplicativity,
\[
\sigma(d)=\sigma(2^i)\sigma(4409^j)\sigma(458009^k).
\]
Consequently, summing independently over the three exponents gives
\[
\sum_{d\mid N}\sigma(d)
 =\left(\sum_{i=0}^{14}\sigma(2^i)\right)
  \left(\sum_{j=0}^{1}\sigma(4409^j)\right)
  \left(\sum_{k=0}^{1}\sigma(458009^k)\right).
\]

For \(i\ge0\),
\[
\sigma(2^i)=1+2+\cdots+2^i=2^{i+1}-1.
\]
It follows that
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{i=0}^{14}\sigma(2^i)
 &=\sum_{i=0}^{14}(2^{i+1}-1)\\
 &=\left(2+2^2+\cdots+2^{15}\right)-15\\
 &=(2^{16}-2)-15\\
 &=65519.
\end{aligned}
\]
For any prime \(p\), \(\sigma(1)=1\) and \(\sigma(p)=1+p\), so
\[
\sum_{j=0}^{1}\sigma(p^j)=1+(1+p)=p+2.
\]
Applying this to the two odd primes gives
\[
\sum_{j=0}^{1}\sigma(4409^j)=4411
\]
and
\[
\sum_{k=0}^{1}\sigma(458009^k)=458011.
\]
Therefore
\[
\sum_{d\mid N}\sigma(d)=65519\cdot4411\cdot458011.
\]
Here
\[
65519\cdot4411=289004309,
\]
and hence
\[
\sum_{d\mid N}\sigma(d)
 =289004309\cdot458011
 =132367152569399.
\]

Substitution into the expression for \(a(N)\) now gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(N)
 &=2\sum_{d\mid N}d-\sum_{d\mid N}\sigma(d)\\
 &=2\cdot66183576284700-132367152569399\\
 &=132367152569400-132367152569399\\
 &=1.
\end{aligned}
\]

Finally, \(N=33085221781504\) is plainly neither \(1\) nor \(12\). If the proposed equivalence
\[
a(n)=1\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad n=1\text{ or }n=12
\]
held for every positive integer \(n\), then applying its forward implication to this \(N\) would yield the disjunction \(N=1\) or \(N=12\). The first case contradicts \(33085221781504\ne1\), and the second contradicts \(33085221781504\ne12\). Thus the proposed equivalence is false.
